# **The PGM Recycling Monitor** _Covering activity in the global automotive recycling sector in H2 2011._ **David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **15 February 2012** _February 2012_ ##### **New York:** - Scrap autocatalyst volumes slipped lower in Q3 compared to Q2 2011 and fell again in Q4 compared to Q3. Declining precious metal and steel prices restricted scrap catalyst flows towards the end of the year. Typically, this sort of price sensitivity is relatively short-lived. • There was little change in the rhodium loadings on scrap catalysts through the final three quarters of 2011. Palladium loadings increased at a faster rate than platinum loadings, reflecting greater use of palladium on gasoline vehicles in North America leading up to 2001. - New car sales are already rising in Japan and should climb further this year as model availability improves during the first few months. Second hand car prices have stopped rising and vehicle scrappage should increase as a result. - In North America, a slow but steady improvement in consumer confidence is helping to boost sales of new vehicles. Scrap rates are rising and more palladium will be recovered as a result. • In Europe, a shaky economy is deterring or delaying purchases of new passenger vehicles. The average age of an in-use car is increasing and scrap rates will fall. Sales of new diesel vehicles should outperform sales of new gasoline cars. With many of these diesel cars replacing old diesel models, platinum collection from scrap catalysts should be stronger than palladium collection. 200 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10166 0130 Tel: +1 212 878 4122 ##### **London:** 4th Floor, St Martins Court, 10 Paternoster Row, London EC4M 7BB Tel: +44 20 7489 6767 ##### **Hong Kong:** Suite 1306, Two Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Central, Hong Kong Tel: +852 2899 2026 ##### **Tokyo:** 2-1 Ohtemachi 1-Chome, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo 100 Tel: +81 33 285 3407 ##### **Singapore:** 80 Robinson Road, #15-02, Singapore, 068898 Tel: +65 6372 8050 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | The PGM Recycling Monitor** **15 February 2012** ## **Refining indicators** Scrap volumes Forecast volumes Optimism Steel prices

Global autocatalyst scrap volumes were a touch lower in Q3 2011 than in Q2 but fell back more substantially in the last three months of the year. Decreasing steel and precious metal prices typically have a short term negative impact on recycling flows. The fall in commodity prices in September therefore had a mild negative effect

on scrap volumes in Q3 and a much more substantial impact on Q4 volumes. Looking forward, there is more optimism from the industry over recycling volumes for the current quarter - price impact can be relatively short-lived - but the outlook for Europe is weaker than for most other regions. _High figures indicate an increase in a measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period. A low figure for the Pt/Pd ratio indicates more palladium in the mix._ The ratio of palladium to platinum recovered from end-of-life and other scrap catalysts continued to move slightly in palladium’s favour. Over the next eighteen months we could see this ratio reaching a plateau, reflecting the peak usage of palladium in the North American automotive market a little over a decade ago. There have been no significant changes in rhodium loadings on recovered catalysts during the last nine month period. Although new car sales were relatively healthy in Q3 and Q4 2011 (positive for recycling), there was no single unified trend around the world. European consumers continued to worry about their economic situation while North American buying strengthened. Some of the faster-growing markets were a little weaker than had been expected: although 2011 sales were higher than a year earlier, Brazilian, Chinese and Indian passenger vehicle sales grew at a slower pace than before. The trend in sales in SE Asia and Japan is complex: while Japanese output and new vehicle registrations showed some recovery from the March disaster, the Thai floods restricted availability of new models in some markets. Used car prices were higher in Q4 than one year earlier in Japan, little-changed in North America and lower in much of Europe. In Japan, a lack of availability of many models for sale following the earthquake and tsunami. This drove additional demand for used vehicles, raising their value and depressing recycling volumes. The slow economic recovery within the USA also encouraged consumers to buy second-hand vehicles. However, the gradual improvement in the domestic economy towards the end of the year has driven new car sales higher. Second hand vehicle prices have stopped rising there and may soon fall, suggesting that scrappage rates and platinum group metal recoveries should rise. 2

#### **Europe:** European metal recovery was down by a few per cent in Q4. As in the other regions, falling metal prices encouraged collectors to hold onto scrap rather than selling it and the weight of pgm

recovered fell. The efforts of the banking system to restore capital ratios has also led to reduced lending which may have made the financing of scrap material more difficult. Continued concerns over Eurozone debt have made many consumers cautious, with car sales being delayed and vehicles scrapped later than would otherwise be the case. Across Europe, the diesel sector is performing more strongly than the gasoline sector. We therefore expect proportionately more scrappage of diesel cars than gasoline models and platinum recoveries to be healthier than palladium recoveries. _High figures indicate an increase in a measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period._ #### **North America:** The US economy has recovered faster than we had previously expected although unemployment remains stubbornly high. While vehicle sales are stronger than they were in early 2011, they remain some way below the peaks of 2005 or 2006. Nonetheless, renewed buying interest from consumers is generally leading to greater metal recoveries from scrapped catalysts. The downturn in metal prices in Q4 did have a negative effect on scrap flows but this was more limited than in Europe. #### **Japan:** Japanese car production recovered well from the March earthquake and tsunami in Q3. By the end of the year, the industry was operating at close to capacity, or would have been if the Thai floods had not disrupted the automotive supply chain once again. By the start of 2012, production had fully returned to normal. As a result of this, the domestic availability of many models was rather limited in the second half of the year. A large number of cars were also damaged during the March events. Together, these factors increased demand for used vehicles and reduced their supply. The number of cars scrapped and the amount of metal recovered fell sharply but should start to grow again as domestic sales firm. #### **Rest of the World:** Metal recoveries from Korea, elsewhere in Asia and the Rest of the World were stronger in Q4 2011 than in Q3 despite weak metal prices. These flows are relatively limited in scale as many vehicles being scrapped in these markets are not fitted with catalysts (because emissions legislation was typically introduced later than in Europe, Japan and North America). The outlook for metal recycled from these regions is positive for 2012. Finally, we note that Anglo American Platinum’s recent annual results presentation revealed that it has started processing secondary (scrap) material to better utilise its smelting and refining capacity. As a major source of secondary material, we believe this is likely to include autocatalyst scrap. 3

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | The PGM Recycling Monitor** **15 February 2012** ## **Notes to methodology** This survey uses similar methodology to previous reports issued by Mitsui Precious Metals on the gold refining market. Mitsui surveys a large number of participants in the autocatalyst recovery sector to obtain semi-quantitative information on the market. This data is then weighted by the significance of the respondent and averaged across the industry. High figures indicate an increase in a measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period. For quantitative figures on demand, we refer the reader to the usual Johnson Matthey and GFMS reports on the platinum group metal market. ## **Timescale** This survey covers autocatalyst recycling activity from July to September and October to December 2011 inclusive (Q3 and Q4 CY 2011). Companies surveyed include collectors, decanners, smelters and refiners. Results therefore reflect slightly different timeframes according to where in the recycling process the respondent fits. Forward-looking forecasts relate to the next three month period while optimism measures longer term views. Backward-looking data is compared to the same period three months earlier. ## **To be involved in this survey** Mitsui currently carries out this surve

y on a quarterly basis but only publishes this report twice a year. All respondents will receive averaged data on a quarterly basis between the published reports as a thank you for their participation in the survey process. We would like to improve the accuracy of this survey and therefore welcome other respondents. If you wish to be involved in this survey, or have any other comments, please contact us at david.jollie@mitprecious.com. ## **Acknowledgements** Mitsui would like to thank all of the companies involved for their suggestions on this report, their time and their kind responses to our questions. 5
